direct_claims: The chart is published by Our World in Data.
It is based on a 2024 study by Harriet Bartlett et al. titled 'Trade-offs in the externalities of pig production are not inevitable'.
The chart plots greenhouse gas emissions against the welfare cost of pig production across 91 different production systems in the United Kingdom and Brazil.
The y-axis measures greenhouse gas emissions in kilograms per kilogram of deadweight pig meat.
The x-axis measures 'welfare cost', where negative values represent a benefit to animal welfare (good) and positive values represent a cost to animal welfare (bad).
Welfare cost is calculated by weighting the quantity of years lived by quality-of-life scores from detailed welfare assessments.
Different production systems are categorized, including Outdoor, Slatted, Slatted + Straw yard, Solid floor, Straw yard, and Straw yard + outdoor.
derived_claims: The purpose is to analyze whether there is an inevitable trade-off between environmental impact (emissions) and animal welfare.

Outdoor systems generally cluster on the left side of the chart, indicating lower (better) welfare costs, but they show a wide variation in emissions, ranging from under 3 kg to over 8 kg of CO2-equivalent per kg deadweight.
Slatted systems cluster on the right side of the chart, indicating higher (worse) welfare costs, but generally have lower emissions, mostly concentrated between 1.5 kg and 5 kg.

This distribution suggests a trade-off where systems with better animal welfare (like outdoor systems) sometimes have higher or more variable carbon footprints, while intensive systems (like slatted floors) have lower carbon footprints but worse animal welfare.
If consumers or policies solely incentivize low-carbon meat, they might inadvertently promote systems with poorer animal welfare (like slatted floors).
Conversely, mandating high-welfare outdoor systems without addressing efficiency could lead to higher greenhouse gas emissions per kilogram of meat produced.

The study's title 'Trade-offs... are not inevitable' suggests that some systems manage to achieve both low emissions and good welfare, as seen by some outdoor systems having emissions around 3 kg, which is comparable to slatted systems.
There is an outlier system ('Straw yard + outdoor') with very high emissions of over 12 kg per kg deadweight.
